Header: Podosphaera leucotricha Amharic: amedaye; Tigrigna: hammokshtay; Oromifa: dakuya

Prevention: When planting a new orchard use proper spacing usually 6 x 6 m (but it depends on the variety)
Prune tree branches to allow air circulation.
Remove all dead and dried branches and shoots at the end of the season and burn.
Use clean pruning equipment to avoid contamination, sterilise by heating in fire
Pick up and bury fallen leaves and fruits 60 cm deep as these can harbour the fungus and help spread the disease in the following season
Keep the orchard weed free to eradicate alternative hosts of this pathogen
In nurseries, avoid overhead watering to reduce the relative humidity as excessive watering increases the incidence of the disease
Monitoring: Before blossoming, mark 5 trees/ha randomly in the orchard and check for symptoms of the disease every week
Primary infection causes the terminal buds to become silver-grey in colour leading to defoliation, stunted growth, and die-back.
The disease spreads to the leaves, blossoms, and fruit.
Secondary symptoms appear on leaves as white/grey felt-like patches, frequently on the underside with yellow patches on the upper surface.
Infected fruit becomes russeted (reddish- brown in colour).
The fruits are smaller and may be deformed
When the primary symptoms are seen, carry out control methods
Direct Control: Prune all dried and infected shoots and all infected plant parts after harvest and burn or bury 60 cm.
Do not compost infected plant debris
Also as the flower buds emerge early in the season, prune any with visible signs of infection
Spray infected shoots with a solution of 6 spoons of baking powder, 3 spoons of white oil and white bar soap foam and mix in 15 litres of water and spray every week to reduce infection
Restrictions: There are no registered fungicides in
Ethiopia for the management of powdery mildew on apples
